blocks.prompt: 8 (i) Prove that in any triangle \(ABC\): \(b = c\cos A + a\cos C\)
blocks.explanation:
A projection law: side \(b\) equals the projections of the other two sides on it.
Plan: write \(\underline{b} = -\underline{a} - \underline{c}\), take the dot product with \(\underline{b}\), and divide by \(b\).
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\) with sides \(a = BC\), \(b = CA\), \(c = AB\).
To prove: \(b = c\cos A + a\cos C\).
Method: Vector form of the triangle and dot products, as in Example 7(ii).

Set up (as in Example 7)
Let \(\underline{a}\), \(\underline{b}\), \(\underline{c}\) lie along \(BC\), \(CA\), \(AB\), so
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
with \(|\underline{a}| = a\), \(|\underline{b}| = b\), \(|\underline{c}| = c\). Placed tail to tail, the angle between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) is \(\pi - A\), so
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{c} = bc\cos(\pi - A) = -bc\cos A\]
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = -ca\cos B\]
\[\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = -ab\cos C\]
Why: Going round the triangle head to tail brings us back to the start, so the sum is the zero vector. Each pair of side vectors meets at an exterior angle, and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).

Dot \(\underline{b} = -\underline{a} - \underline{c}\) with \(\underline{b}\)
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{b} = -\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} - \underline{c}\cdot\underline{b}\]
\[b^2 = ab\cos C + bc\cos A\]
Why: \(\underline{b}\cdot\underline{b} = b^2\); \(-\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = ab\cos C\) and \(-\underline{c}\cdot\underline{b} = bc\cos A\) from the set-up.

Divide by \(b\)
\[b = a\cos C + c\cos A\]
Why: \(b \ne 0\) (a side of a triangle).

Check
\[\text{Equilateral, side 1:}\]
\[1 = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} \;\checkmark\]
Why: All angles \(60^{\circ}\), \(\cos 60^{\circ} = \tfrac{1}{2}\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(b = c\cos A + a\cos C\).

blocks.prompt: 8 (ii) Prove that in any triangle \(ABC\): \(c = a\cos B + b\cos A\)
blocks.explanation:
The projection law for side \(c\).
Plan: write \(\underline{c} = -\underline{a} - \underline{b}\), dot with \(\underline{c}\), divide by \(c\).
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\).
To prove: \(c = a\cos B + b\cos A\).
Method: Same as part (i), now isolating \(\underline{c}\).

Set up (as in Example 7)
Let \(\underline{a}\), \(\underline{b}\), \(\underline{c}\) lie along \(BC\), \(CA\), \(AB\), so
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
with \(|\underline{a}| = a\), \(|\underline{b}| = b\), \(|\underline{c}| = c\). Placed tail to tail, the angle between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) is \(\pi - A\), so
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{c} = bc\cos(\pi - A) = -bc\cos A\]
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = -ca\cos B\]
\[\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = -ab\cos C\]
Why: Going round the triangle head to tail brings us back to the start, so the sum is the zero vector. Each pair of side vectors meets at an exterior angle, and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).

Dot \(\underline{c} = -\underline{a} - \underline{b}\) with \(\underline{c}\)
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{c} = -\underline{a}\cdot\underline{c} - \underline{b}\cdot\underline{c}\]
\[c^2 = ca\cos B + bc\cos A\]
Why: \(-\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = ca\cos B\) and \(-\underline{b}\cdot\underline{c} = bc\cos A\) from the set-up.

Divide by \(c\)
\[c = a\cos B + b\cos A\]
Why: \(c \ne 0\).

Check
\[\text{Right angle at } C:\]
\[a = 3,\ b = 4,\ c = 5\]
\[3 \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} + 4 \cdot \tfrac{4}{5}\]
\[= \tfrac{25}{5} = 5 \;\checkmark\]
Why: \(\cos B = a/c = 3/5\), \(\cos A = b/c = 4/5\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(c = a\cos B + b\cos A\).

blocks.prompt: 8 (iii) Prove that in any triangle \(ABC\): \(b^2 = c^2 + a^2 - 2ca\cos B\)
blocks.explanation:
The cosine law for side \(b\).
Plan: write \(\underline{b} = -(\underline{c} + \underline{a})\) and take the dot product of each side with itself.
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\).
To prove: \(b^2 = c^2 + a^2 - 2ca\cos B\).
Method: As in Example 7(i): square the vector equation using the dot product.

Set up (as in Example 7)
Let \(\underline{a}\), \(\underline{b}\), \(\underline{c}\) lie along \(BC\), \(CA\), \(AB\), so
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
with \(|\underline{a}| = a\), \(|\underline{b}| = b\), \(|\underline{c}| = c\). Placed tail to tail, the angle between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) is \(\pi - A\), so
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{c} = bc\cos(\pi - A) = -bc\cos A\]
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = -ca\cos B\]
\[\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = -ab\cos C\]
Why: Going round the triangle head to tail brings us back to the start, so the sum is the zero vector. Each pair of side vectors meets at an exterior angle, and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).

Dot \(\underline{b} = -(\underline{c} + \underline{a})\) with itself
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{b} = (\underline{c} + \underline{a})\cdot(\underline{c} + \underline{a})\]
\[= \underline{c}\cdot\underline{c} + 2\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} + \underline{a}\cdot\underline{a}\]
Why: The two minus signs multiply to plus; \(\underline{a}\cdot\underline{c} = \underline{c}\cdot\underline{a}\) (commutative), so the middle terms combine.

Use the set-up
\[b^2 = c^2 + 2(-ca\cos B) + a^2\]
\[= c^2 + a^2 - 2ca\cos B\]
Why: \(\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = -ca\cos B\).

Check
\[B = 90^{\circ}:\ b^2 = c^2 + a^2\]
Why: \(\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\) gives Pythagoras, as it should (\(b\) is then the hypotenuse).

blocks.prompt: 8 (iv) Prove that in any triangle \(ABC\): \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\)
blocks.explanation:
The cosine law for side \(c\).
Plan: write \(\underline{c} = -(\underline{a} + \underline{b})\) and dot each side with itself.
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\).
To prove: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\).
Method: Same as part (iii).

Set up (as in Example 7)
Let \(\underline{a}\), \(\underline{b}\), \(\underline{c}\) lie along \(BC\), \(CA\), \(AB\), so
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
with \(|\underline{a}| = a\), \(|\underline{b}| = b\), \(|\underline{c}| = c\). Placed tail to tail, the angle between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) is \(\pi - A\), so
\[\underline{b}\cdot\underline{c} = bc\cos(\pi - A) = -bc\cos A\]
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{a} = -ca\cos B\]
\[\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = -ab\cos C\]
Why: Going round the triangle head to tail brings us back to the start, so the sum is the zero vector. Each pair of side vectors meets at an exterior angle, and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).

Dot \(\underline{c} = -(\underline{a} + \underline{b})\) with itself
\[\underline{c}\cdot\underline{c} = (\underline{a} + \underline{b})\cdot(\underline{a} + \underline{b})\]
\[= \underline{a}\cdot\underline{a} + 2\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} + \underline{b}\cdot\underline{b}\]
Why: Expand; \(\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = \underline{b}\cdot\underline{a}\).

Use the set-up
\[c^2 = a^2 + 2(-ab\cos C) + b^2\]
\[= a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\]
Why: \(\underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = -ab\cos C\).

Check
\[a = b = c,\ C = 60^{\circ}:\]
\[a^2 + a^2 - 2a^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = a^2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: In an equilateral triangle \(C = 60^{\circ}\).
